prompt: A listing broker's primary fiduciary duty to the seller client is to:

options.text: Promote the seller's interests with loyalty, care, and obedience within the law
Obtain the highest possible price even when the seller directs a quicker sale
Treat buyer and seller with equal advocacy so both receive fair representation
Advise the seller on title and tax matters as the seller's legal representative

explanation: Agency duties center on loyalty and obedience to lawful client instructions, not guaranteeing outcomes.

distractorExplanations.b: Price is not the top duty; obedience requires following the seller's lawful instruction to favor a quick sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Equal advocacy describes a neutral or dual role; a listing broker owes loyalty to the seller client, not both sides.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses agency with legal practice; a broker must refer title and tax questions to an attorney or CPA.

prompt: When must a licensee typically disclose a dual agency or designated agency relationship?

options.text: At closing, when the settlement agent reviews the final agency paperwork
Before or as soon as practicable when the dual/designated relationship arises
Once the purchase contract is accepted and both parties have signed it
Only if one of the parties is an existing client rather than a customer

explanation: Agency disclosure timing is early—when the dual or designated relationship is created or contemplated. Exact timing follows the applicable license-law rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Closing is far too late; informed consent must come before the licensee acts for both parties.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting until acceptance means both parties negotiated without knowing the licensee's divided loyalty.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosure is triggered by the dual or designated relationship itself, not by whether a party was a prior client.

prompt: An exclusive right-to-sell listing generally means:

options.text: The listing broker is owed a commission unless the seller personally finds the buyer during the term
The seller may list with several brokers and pays a commission only to the broker who procures the buyer
The listing broker is owed a commission if the property sells during the term, regardless of who finds the buyer
The broker keeps any sale proceeds above the seller's stated minimum price as the commission

explanation: Exclusive right-to-sell typically protects the listing broker's commission if a sale occurs during the listing term. The exact protection follows the terms of the listing agreement.

distractorExplanations.a: That describes an exclusive agency listing, where the seller keeps the right to sell without owing a commission.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes an open listing, where only the procuring broker is paid and the seller may also sell directly.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a net listing, which concerns how the commission is calculated, not exclusivity of the right to sell.

prompt: Listing agent Beth, whose Mobile listing agreement does not authorize her to sign contracts, accepts a buyer's offer for traveling seller Jim. On his return, Jim reviews the terms and signs a written approval of the deal. How did Beth gain authority?

options.text: By ratification, through Jim's approval after the fact
By ostensible agency, since the buyer trusted Beth's title
By express agency created when Beth signed the acceptance
By the listing agreement, which lets agents bind sellers

explanation: Ratification creates agency after the fact: when a principal knowingly approves an act done without authority, the act binds him as if it had been authorized from the start. Jim reviewed and approved Beth's unauthorized acceptance in writing. Ostensible agency instead rests on the principal's earlier conduct leading a third party to believe authority existed.

distractorExplanations.b: Ostensible agency comes from the principal's own conduct creating apparent authority before the act; here Jim's later approval bound him.
distractorExplanations.c: Express agency is granted by the principal in advance. Beth's own act of signing cannot give her authority she lacked.
distractorExplanations.d: A typical listing hires the broker to find a buyer; it does not authorize signing contracts that bind the seller.

prompt: A net listing arrangement is often risky or restricted because

prompt: Seller Ruth's purchase contract lists no exclusions. Before closing she removes a custom wall bookcase bolted into a niche built for it, saying she always meant to take it. The buyer objects. Who most likely is entitled to the bookcase?

options.text: Ruth, because her intention to remove it controls
Ruth, since bookcases are furniture and stay personal property
Ruth, because removing it before closing ends the buyer's claim
The buyer, since attachment and custom fit make it a fixture

explanation: Courts apply the fixture tests: method of attachment, adaptation to the property, relationship of the parties, intent shown objectively, and the parties' agreement. The bookcase is bolted in and built for that niche, and the contract excludes nothing, so it conveys with the real estate. A seller's unstated intent does not override those facts.

distractorExplanations.a: Intent is judged by objective facts such as attachment and adaptation, not by a private plan Ruth never put in the contract.
distractorExplanations.b: Freestanding furniture is personal property, but a bookcase bolted into a custom niche has become part of the real estate.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing a fixture before closing does not defeat the buyer's right; the buyer may demand it back or seek its value.

prompt: An Alabama licensee helps a first-time buyer tour homes and write an offer, but they never sign a written agency agreement. The buyer later claims the licensee owed her loyalty as her agent. Under RECAD, what was the relationship?

options.text: Single agent for the buyer, created by helping write the offer
Transaction broker, as no written agency agreement exists
Subagent of the listing broker, the default under state law
Dual agent for both the buyer and the seller in the deal

explanation: Under Alabama's Real Estate Consumer's Agency and Disclosure Act (RECAD), a licensee is treated as a transaction broker, assisting without representing either party, unless a written agreement establishes an agency relationship. Touring homes and writing an offer did not create buyer agency here.

distractorExplanations.a: Helping with tours and an offer does not create single agency under RECAD; that relationship requires a written agreement.
distractorExplanations.c: Subagency is not the RECAD default; the default is transaction broker, which represents neither side.
distractorExplanations.d: Dual agency requires informed written consent from both parties; with no written agreement at all, the licensee is a transaction broker.
